issues.subcategory: Validity of mirrored letters as novel stimuli
issues.description: Validity of mirrored letters as novel stimuli: The authors operationalize "pseudo-letters" by mirror-reversing standard letters, subsequently referring to them as "novel stimuli" in the discussion. However, mirror-reversed letters are not strictly novel; they are familiar objects presented in an atypical orientation. The visual system possesses robust mechanisms for orientation invariance and mental rotation, which may process these stimuli differently than genuinely novel, unnamable shapes. The authors should discuss the limitations of using mirrored letters as a proxy for novel stimuli and address how orientation-invariant visual processing might contribute to the observed pseudo-to-real memory errors.

issues.subcategory: Ambiguous definition of high confidence threshold
issues.description: Ambiguous definition of high confidence threshold: The authors base their primary analyses and conclusions on "high confidence" trials to distinguish true memory illusions from guesses. However, the manuscript does not explicitly define which points on the 4-point confidence scale were categorized as "high confidence" for the analyses (e.g., only responses rated '4', or responses rated '3' and '4'). Please specify the exact threshold used to classify a response as high confidence to ensure the methodology is transparent and reproducible.

issues.subcategory: Confounding verbal encoding in visual memory
issues.description: Confounding verbal encoding in visual memory: The manuscript relies on letters to probe short-term memory, but letters are highly verbalizable stimuli. Because the experimental design did not utilize articulatory suppression, it is highly probable that participants employed verbal rehearsal strategies (e.g., encoding a mirrored 'C' as the verbal concept "C" plus a "mirrored" tag). If the supplementary "mirrored" tag decays more rapidly than the primary verbal identity, the resulting error would manifest as a pseudo-to-real illusion. The authors should explicitly discuss the lack of articulatory suppression as a limitation that complicates the interpretation of these errors as purely visual memory illusions, and contextualize this within established models of working memory where visual and verbal codes interact.

issues.subcategory: Omission of classic reconstructive memory literature
issues.description: Omission of classic reconstructive memory literature: The conclusion that recent visual memories are shaped by world knowledge and expectations aligns closely with foundational work on reconstructive memory and schema theory, yet this classic literature is largely absent from the discussion. Studies dating back to Carmichael, Hogan, and Walter (1932) have demonstrated how verbal labels and prior knowledge systematically distort the recall of visual forms. Integrating these classic perspectives would provide a more comprehensive theoretical foundation for the observed phenomena, bridging historical schema theories with the modern predictive processing framework proposed by the authors.

issues.subcategory: Absence of data and code availability
issues.description: Absence of data and code availability: The manuscript does not contain a data or code availability statement. To ensure the reproducibility of the findings and allow independent verification of the Bayesian ANOVA models, the raw data, JASP analysis files, and the custom MATLAB/Psychophysics Toolbox experimental scripts must be made available in a persistent public repository.

issues.subcategory: High participant exclusion rate introduces bias
issues.description: High participant exclusion rate introduces bias: The exclusion of 17 out of 40 participants (42.5%) in Experiment 1 and 92 out of 290 participants (31.7%) in Experiment 2 based on having 10 or fewer high-confidence trials is exceptionally high. Excluding such a large proportion of the sample based on a performance-dependent metric (confidence) introduces a severe risk of selection bias, as the remaining participants may not be representative of the general population. The authors should report a sensitivity analysis including all participants (perhaps using a mixed-effects model that can handle variable trial counts) or justify why this massive exclusion does not bias the primary conclusions.

issues.subcategory: Missing measures of variability for error rates
issues.description: Missing measures of variability for error rates: Throughout the manuscript, the authors report point estimates for error rates (e.g., percentages of illusory errors) but fail to report any measures of variability, such as standard deviations, standard errors, or Bayesian credible intervals. Providing only point estimates prevents readers from assessing the precision of these estimates and the overlap between conditions. Please include appropriate measures of dispersion for all reported summary statistics in the text.

issues.subcategory: Incomplete description of sequential stopping rule
issues.description: Incomplete description of sequential stopping rule: The stopping rule for Experiments 3 and 4 is incompletely specified. While Bayesian sequential testing is robust to optional stopping, a rigorous pre-planned design should specify a minimum sample size before the first look, a maximum sample size (to prevent infinite data collection if the BF hovers near 1), and a stopping rule for evidence supporting the null hypothesis (e.g., BF < 0.1). Please clarify whether these parameters were established prior to data collection and report them to ensure methodological transparency.

issues.description: Missing zero-delay perceptual control: The authors argue that the observed errors are memory-based rather than perceptual because they increase over time. However, even at the shortest delays (0.5s or 0.75s), the expectation-induced error rate is substantial (e.g., 25% for pseudo-letters in Experiment 2). To definitively rule out perceptual illusions or encoding errors as the primary driver of these baseline errors, a 0-second delay or simultaneous matching control condition is necessary. Without this baseline, it is difficult to isolate the exact proportion of errors attributable to memory maintenance versus initial perceptual encoding.

issues.description: Unjustified conclusion from null effect: The authors interpret the null effect of cue color in Experiment 2 as evidence that expectations require substantial time to develop. This conclusion is not logically supported by the data. The lack of an effect could equally be attributed to an ineffective cueing paradigm, participants ignoring the cue, or the transient cue being too weak to override the highly overlearned, lifelong prior for real letters. I recommend revising this statement to acknowledge these alternative methodological explanations rather than drawing a definitive mechanistic conclusion from a null result.

issues.description: Table 4 contradicts prose on non-illusory errors: The text states that for non-illusory errors, "only Memory Delay was a relevant factor" and cites a BFincl of 190 for Memory Delay. However, Table 4 shows that Memory Delay has a BFincl of 0.064 (indicating it is not a relevant factor), while Target Type has a BFincl of 39110.895.
issues.quote: For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42, see Appendix 1 for a full model comparison and Table 4 for an overview of BFincl for each model component).

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent pseudo-letter target proportion for Experiment 2
issues.description: Inconsistent pseudo-letter target proportion for Experiment 2: The introduction to Experiment 3 states that pseudo-letters made up 33% of the targets in Experiment 2. However, the Methods section for Experiment 2 states that a pseudo-letter was the target on 25% of trials with a red cue and 60% of trials with a blue cue. Assuming the two cue colors were equally intermixed (as implied by the text), this would average to 42.5%, not 33%.
